topic.title: Salary secrecy only ever protected the company
topic.claim: Younger colleagues telling each other their salaries feels rude to older managers, and it's one of the best things happening in offices.
topic.moment: Two juniors compare offer letters over lunch and one realises she's paid less for the same work.

turn.believed: Talking about salary is unprofessional and causes trouble.
turn.actually: Secrecy let companies pay people differently for the same job, and silence helped only them.

topic.because: When nobody knows the range, nobody can ask for it. Sharing numbers gives workers the one thing HR always had.
topic.payoff: If your company discourages salary talk, ask who benefits from you not knowing.
topic.behaviour: Young employees share pay openly with peers and on anonymous apps.
topic.mechanism: Information was the company's leverage, and sharing it moves leverage to workers.
topic.send_to: The colleague who thinks asking a peer's salary is bad manners.
topic.why_now: Appraisal season is when these lunch conversations happen most.
real_details: A thread asked people to share role, first salary, current salary and age so salary figures come with the journey behind them.
The poster started with their own: product designer, ₹3 LPA first salary, ₹35 LPA now, age 28.
They noted that it might take 10 years or 3 years with 6 job switches to reach a high salary, so context matters.
The post got a bigger response than they expected.

score.why: Salary secrecy only ever helped the company. The genuinely good side of a generational shift.

topic.villain: a pay-secrecy norm that keeps salary ranges hidden from the people earning them

cover.headline: Comparing salaries with colleagues feels rude. [It's the best habit] in offices.
cover.sub: The silence was always worth money to one side of the table.

paragraphs: Comparing salaries with colleagues feels rude. It's the best habit in offices.
slides.why_swipe: Why would something that feels rude be good for you?

paragraphs: It's your first year. Same team, same role, you even joined the same week.
Lunch at the cafeteria, both of you moaning about appraisal forms. Then your batchmate leans in, drops their voice, glances at the next table: "What's your CTC, by the way?"
slides.why_swipe: What happens when the numbers come out?

paragraphs: You say yours. They say theirs. Theirs is higher by roughly your rent.
Your ears go warm. For a second you feel stupid for even answering, like you broke a rule nobody ever wrote down. You hear yourself say "achha, nice" and start talking about the canteen paneer.
Your spoon sits in the dal, and the cafeteria noise suddenly sounds very loud.
slides.why_swipe: So what does that gap actually mean?

paragraphs: But that night you open your offer letter again. The number looks smaller than it did this morning.
Maybe they pushed harder, or their last job paid more. You can't tell, because neither of you ever saw the range. You can't ask for a number you've never seen.
**HR always had everyone's number. You only had your own.**
slides.why_swipe: So what does that do to your next raise?

paragraphs: So the appraisal mail arrives with a modest hike. You reply "thank you so much" with a smiley.
With no range to check, you measure the hike against your own old salary. Against that, it looks generous.
I've watched friends say thank you for hikes like this, and mean it.
slides.why_swipe: So why does salary talk still get called rude?

paragraphs: Your manager still calls salary talk bad manners.
**It's the one office rule that only protects whoever already knows everyone's number.**
Somewhere upstairs sits a spreadsheet with both your names in it, one row apart.

end.save: Read it again the week before your appraisal meeting.
end.send: Send to the colleague who still thinks asking a peer's salary is bad manners.

draft.caption: One CTC shared over cafeteria lunch teaches you more than every appraisal form put together.
draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel. The cover says comparing salaries with colleagues feels rude but is the best habit in offices. The slides follow a reader at a cafeteria lunch in their first year. A batchmate in the same role, who joined the same week, lowers their voice and asks the reader's CTC. Theirs is higher by about the reader's rent. The reader's ears go warm, they say 'achha, nice' and change the subject. That night they reread their offer letter and realise they can't tell why the gap exists, because neither of them ever saw the salary range. Later a modest hike looks generous, because it is only measured against their own old salary. The post ends saying calling salary talk bad manners only protects whoever already knows everyone's number, with an image of a spreadsheet holding both names one row apart.
